content: Nicocodeine, marketed under brand names such as Lyopect® and Tusscodin®, is an opiate derivative that is structurally related to dihydrocodeine and is the codeine analogue of nicomorphine. It was developed for use as both a cough suppressant and an analgesic. This compound is not widely utilized in most countries, although its pharmacological activity is comparable to other opiates. Nicocodeine, along with nicomorphine, was introduced in the late 1950s by Lannacher Heilmittel, an Austrian pharmaceutical company. In the liver, nicocodeine undergoes metabolism through demethylation, resulting in the production of nicomorphine, also known as 6-nicotinoylmorphine. Nicomorphine is subsequently metabolized further into morphine. The side effects of nicocodeine are similar to those observed with other opiates and include itching, nausea, and respiratory depression. Nicocodeine is regulated in a manner similar to codeine and other weak opiate drugs, such as ethylmorphine, benzylmorphine, dihydrocodeine, and its derivatives like acetyldihydrocodeine. However, stronger opiates such as hydrocodone and oxycodone are regulated more stringently, akin to morphine. These regulations are consistent across various national laws and international agreements, such as the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. In the United States, nicocodeine is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, alongside heroin. This classification reflects the fact that nicocodeine was never introduced for medical use in the United States. A related compound, nicodicodeine, is to nicocodeine what codeine is to dihydrocodeine. The metabolism of nicodicodeine produces dihydromorphine, whereas nicocodeine is metabolized into morphine, as previously described. Nicocodeine-based cough medications are available in various formulations, including syrups, extended-release syrups, and sublingual drops. Analgesic preparations are also available in the form of sublingual drops and oral tablets. The potency of nicocodeine is approximately equivalent to that of hydrocodone.
